case_studies.title: GreyZone: Production-quality Agentic Application Threats
case_studies.abstract: Agents are increasingly deployed across domains such as coding, banking, and commerce. Their ability to invoke tools and change application state makes security testing important for reliable deployment. Although agent security has been studied through various adversarial testing approaches, benchmarks grounded in production agent environments remain limited. We introduce GreyZone, a benchmark for evaluating automated red-teaming services against real-world agent applications. Unlike benchmarks such as AgentDojo, which primarily evaluate subject agents under attack, GreyZone evaluates services' ability to generate and deliver attacks that cause verified security-policy violations. We select independently developed, open-source agent applications with security boundaries concerning access permissions, confidentiality, and action authorization. These applications expose diverse attack surfaces, including those arising from multi-agent interactions and multimodal inputs. By grounding evaluation in application environments that preserve production-relevant workflows and independently verifying outcomes, GreyZone supports research on automated agent security testing. Specifically, we present two preliminary case studies using Promptfoo on Letta Code and Clawith to examine attack delivery, agent behavior, and verified outcomes. We release the benchmark, including subject agents and attack surfaces for each application, to support further research on agent testing methods.
case_studies.summary: GreyZone is a benchmark that tests automated red‑team tools on real, production‑grade agent applications. It checks whether a testing service can generate attacks that breach the agents’ security policies and confirms the violations. The study shows that existing red‑team tools can successfully exploit open‑source agents, highlighting gaps in their security controls.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, check if your agents expose any of the GreyZone test cases: 1) run the GreyZone benchmark against your agent stack, 2) verify that your security policies are enforced in the test environment, 3) patch any vulnerabilities discovered before deploying to production.
case_studies.score_reasoning: GreyZone provides a production-quality benchmark for automated red‑team testing of agentic applications, directly relevant to IT engineers managing SaaS, cloud, and endpoint security. The authors released the benchmark, subject agents, and attack surfaces, making it a usable, testable system. The framework can be immediately integrated into existing security workflows, offering a concrete service that can be commercialised or applied internally within 90 days.

case_studies.title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design
case_studies.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.
case_studies.summary: BitDecoding‑FP4 tackles the accuracy‑bandwidth trade‑off in 4‑bit KV cache decoding for LLMs by combining new quantisation tricks with hardware‑level softmax optimisation. It delivers near‑BF16 accuracy while boosting serving throughput 2.4–3× on NVIDIA GPUs. This is relevant for cloud infra that hosts large‑context LLMs, offering a way to reduce memory use and increase performance.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage GPU‑based LLM serving, check if your KV cache uses 4‑bit formats: 1) integrate BitDecoding‑FP4’s dual‑residual query quantisation and outlier‑aware key quantisation into your model export; 2) enable transposed softmax with fused probability quantisation on your GPU kernel; 3) benchmark throughput against BF16 to confirm the 2–3× gain.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical, code‑available method for efficient 4‑bit KV caching in LLM serving, directly impacting cloud‑based LLM deployments. The implementation is released and demonstrably works, making it ready for deployment. IT engineers can integrate it into existing LLM pipelines to boost throughput and reduce GPU memory usage, offering tangible monetisation potential. Overall, the work scores high on all criteria for an infrastructure‑focused audience.

case_studies.title: FOSCAR: Accelerating Decode Attention over 2- and 4-Bit KV Caches through Affine Folding
case_studies.abstract: Large-language-model decode attention streams the key-value (KV) cache for every generated token. Packing that cache into 2-bit or 4-bit quantized integers reduces memory traffic but does not automatically translate into latency saving. Existing 2-bit fused kernels reach under 31%/15% of peak HBM throughput on H100/B200. Converting each value and applying its scale and offset before feeding Tensor Cores is a major bottleneck because instruction-issue throughput is scarce on modern GPUs. Instead of applying scale and offset to each KV value, FOSCAR uses affine folding to apply them to the other operand or the output of decode-attention matrix products, depending on the quantization scheme (token-wise or channel-wise). This reduces scale-and-offset operations by up to two orders of magnitude while preserving the dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic. FOSCAR also uses bit manipulation to feed KV operands to Tensor Cores efficiently, requiring only 1 and 0.19 ALU instructions per INT2 element on H100 and B200, respectively. Finally, FOSCAR builds warp-specialized GPU pipelines for Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) using wgmma and tcgen05. On H100, FOSCAR INT2 and INT4 kernels achieve geo-mean speedups of $3.36\times$ and $2.83\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, and $2.03\times$ and $1.71\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8. On B200, the corresponding INT2 and INT4 speedups are $2.67\times$ and $2.30\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, $1.48\times$ and $1.28\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8, and $1.16\times$ and $1.00\times$ over TensorRT-LLM NVFP4. We integrate FOSCAR into SGLang to benchmark serving efficiency. On long-context serving workloads, FOSCAR increases peak aggregate throughput by up to 170% and 341% over 2-bit and 16-bit baselines, respectively. We open-source FOSCAR as a kernel library at https://github.com/FutureMLS-Lab/FOSCAR.
case_studies.summary: FOSCAR tackles the slow decoding of large‑language models by using affine folding to skip costly scale‑and‑offset operations on 2‑bit and 4‑bit key‑value caches, and by packing these values efficiently for Tensor Cores. The authors built highly specialised GPU pipelines for Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) that deliver 2–3× speedups over existing FP8 and BF16 solutions, boosting long‑context serving throughput by up to 341%.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a highly optimized GPU kernel library (FOSCAR) for reducing KV cache quantization overhead in LLM decode attention, directly impacting LLM deployment performance on modern NVIDIA GPUs. The implementation is open‑source and integrated into a production‑grade serving framework (SGLang), indicating practical readiness. While the immediate monetisation is mainly for in‑house LLM serving or as a performance component in managed LLM services, the solution is actionable within 90 days for engineers with access to H100/B200 GPUs.

case_studies.title: Intent-Aware Caching for Efficient LLM Serving
case_studies.abstract: Modern LLM serving systems use prefix caching to accelerate multi-turn conversational workloads. They cache the key-value states of previous conversation prefixes and reuse them when subsequent requests share the same prefix, to avoid redundant prefill computation and reduce serving latency. However, achieving a high cache hit rate remains challenging because cache reuse depends on whether a conversation continues and how soon the next turn arrives. Our analysis of real workloads shows that user intent is a useful signal for this behavior, as different intents exhibit different continuation probabilities and inter-turn delays. Based on this key insight, we propose Intent-Aware Caching (IAC), an online eviction policy that classifies requests by intent, learns lightweight reuse statistics from recent serving logs and leverages these statistics to guide an oracle-inspired eviction strategy. Extensive evaluation on real workloads (WildChat and ShareChat) shows that IAC reaches a 34.6% cache hit rate. This substantially outperforms both the previous learning-based approach (18.8%) and traditional methods such as least recently used (LRU, 12.2%), while reducing average serving latency by up to 46.1%.
case_studies.summary: The research tackles the low hit‑rate problem in LLM prefix caching by using user intent to predict when a conversation will continue. They built an online eviction policy that classifies requests by intent, learns reuse stats, and evicts based on those stats, achieving a 34.6% hit‑rate and up to 46% lower latency. This directly benefits cloud‑based LLM services, improving resource utilisation and response times.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM inference infrastructure, implement an intent‑aware cache: 1) add a lightweight intent classifier to your request pipeline, 2) log recent intent‑specific reuse patterns, 3) adapt your cache eviction policy to favour prefixes from intents with high continuation rates.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a practical caching strategy for LLM serving that directly benefits infrastructure engineers handling LLM deployments, with measurable latency improvements. The approach appears to be implemented and evaluated, indicating reasonable maturity. It offers a clear, deployable method that could be integrated into existing serving stacks or sold as a performance optimisation service, warranting a high monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: When Instruction Files Go Stale: Documentation Debt and Hidden Cost in Coding Agents
case_studies.abstract: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code are guided by repository instruction files (also called context files or agent configuration files) like AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, which are read in every agent session. As any documentation artifact, these files can fall behind the code and become stale (e.g., a test folder moves, but the file still points to the old one). In technical debt terms, such a stale instruction is documentation debt, and its interest is the cost it adds to every later agent session. Evaluations that check only task success can miss this cost, and the stale file can persist. In this study, we ask what leads agents to act on a stale instruction, how it affects their behavior and at what cost, and how they recover. We study three real-world stale instructions from active open-source repositories in depth, each a different kind of guidance: a test command, a code location, and a procedure for adding a component. Agents fix 22 maintenance tasks under three versions of each instruction (left stale, corrected to the current path, and removed), with the code and the task held fixed, and we analyze 732 trajectories of two models at the level of individual tool calls. We find that agents follow stale guidance when it is relevant to their tasks, sometimes even when correct information is available elsewhere. On the stale test command, Claude Sonnet 5.5 needed about two extra tool calls per run, a third more than with the corrected command; in the other cases, we could not detect a difference. Although agents generally recovered from the immediate failures, none repaired the underlying instruction file. Correcting the instructions eliminated operations on obsolete paths, while removing them prevented most. Our findings show that task success alone can hide the costs of documentation debt, highlighting the need to evaluate agent behavior beyond final outcomes.
case_studies.summary: Stale instruction files cause coding agents to make extra tool calls, adding hidden cost to every run. The authors analysed three real‑world cases, showing that correcting or removing stale docs cuts unnecessary operations. For cloud infra managers, this means keeping agent configs up to date can save time and reduce waste.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI‑powered coding agents, here is what to do: 1) Regularly audit and update your instruction files (e.g., AGENTS.md) to match current repo structure. 2) Remove obsolete sections rather than leaving them stale. 3) Monitor agent run logs for extra tool calls that may indicate stale guidance.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper discusses practical issues with LLM-based coding agents that are directly relevant to software engineering workflows. The findings are based on empirical experiments with existing models (Claude Sonnet 5.5) and real-world repositories, indicating a mature system rather than a theoretical proposal. The insights can be turned into actionable tooling to detect and mitigate stale instruction files, offering a clear monetisation path within 90 days. Overall impact, maturity, and monetisation potential are moderate, leading to a solid score above the 30 threshold.
